video_title: Why Jev Is Changing How We Build With AI
gist: Diego Almeida, ex-OpenAI InstructGPT/RLHF researcher and CEO of Typesafe, argues that LLMs are 'super smart yet useless' for automation because they are optimized for strings consumed by humans, and that Jev, trained via a new objective (RLCD) for calibrated decisions on top of Frankensteined open-weight models, is the start of 'machine native intelligence' that software can depend on. He dismisses the 'it's just a classifier' critique and fast copycats (including OpenAI's newly announced decision models) as missing the point: the moat is calibrated intelligence and reliability, not speed, cost, or interface.

themes.theme: Why LLMs fail at automation: you get what you optimize for

insights.claim: Typesafe's CEO argues the main reason AI can solve hard math but cannot automate accounting, data entry, or insurance underwriting is that LLMs are optimized for strings consumed by humans, while automation requires discrete, field-level decisions consumed by software.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames a large untapped automation market (back-office, underwriting, data entry) that current LLM vendors structurally underserve; watch for decision-optimized model vendors winning enterprise workflow budgets.
insights.quote: all the string LLMs have been optimized for strings and strings are meant to be consumed by humans or other LLMs

insights.claim: Almeida claims AI labs are strongly incentivized not to answer truthfully why their models are superhuman at some tasks but unusable for simple automation despite enormous financial incentive.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals skepticism toward frontier-lab narratives about agentic automation readiness; temper expectations for near-term enterprise automation revenue from general LLMs.
insights.quote: the AI labs are very incentivized to not answer that truthfully

insights.claim: Almeida argues that jaggedness is not intrinsic to LLMs but a product of the optimization process: RLHF makes models reliably avoid things that are easy to punish (e.g. rudeness, word salad), showing post-training can make specific behaviors near-perfectly reliable.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Implies reliability on business decisions is a solvable training-objective problem rather than a capability ceiling, supporting the case for specialized post-training startups.
insights.quote: I would say that jaggedness is not intrinsic to LLM or AI.

insights.claim: The host noted that even Anthropic's customer support agent is good at surfacing FAQs but cannot complete simple tasks like changing a credit card, illustrating the gap between AI demos and usable automation.
insights.speaker: Sam Charrington (host)
insights.so_what: Customer service automation remains unsolved even at frontier labs; be skeptical of customer-service AI vendors' claims of full automation.

insights.claim: Almeida says OpenAI has been showing customer service demos since around 2020, roughly six years ago, yet customer service and even drive-through ordering remain unautomated, which he argues looks easier than Millennium Prize math problems.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Demos run years ahead of reliable deployment; discount demo-driven valuations in customer-service and voice-ordering AI.
insights.quote: demos will always be significantly ahead of the curve

insights.claim: Almeida describes a cynical but rational AI-startup loop: make a demo, raise a seed or Series A, promise reliability, never achieve it, and pivot to a human-in-the-loop product instead of real automation, because current models are not reliable.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Useful diligence lens for AI application startups: check whether 'automation' quietly became human-in-the-loop, which changes margins and scalability.
insights.quote: make a demo raise like a cedar series A say that you're going to make it reliable never end up making that reliable pivot into a human in the loop version

insights.claim: Almeida says he knows of no one who runs an LLM as a true separate software dependency, because LLMs cannot provide abstraction: they break arbitrarily, refuse topics, or silently fall back to other models, which is fine for first-party apps but nonsensical for a developer platform.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Highlights a reliability gap in LLM APIs as developer infrastructure; vendors offering predictable, versioned, abstraction-safe behavior could capture backend workloads.
insights.quote: you can't get abstraction with an LM, right? It can just break arbitrarily

insights.claim: Almeida says there is broad dislike of AI and that the field should own up to why, tying it to AI being the greatest compression of intelligence while having the least utility.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Public backlash risk is linked to a utility gap; products delivering reliable, boring automation may face less resistance than consumer-facing generative AI.
insights.quote: the greatest compression of intelligence while having like the least utility

themes.theme: Data and task over compute: the 'bitterest lesson'

insights.claim: Almeida's 'bitterest lesson' framework amends Sutton's bitter lesson: data matters more than compute, and choosing the right task (training objective) matters more than data, because you get what you optimize for.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Suggests step-change AI value can come from small teams defining new tasks, not just capex-heavy scaling; implies non-hyperscaler model startups can create outsized value.
insights.quote: I believe that data matters a lot more than compute. So you actually need data to put the compute on and more important than data is you need the right task.

insights.claim: Almeida says the giant jumps in ML (ChatGPT, o1, and he argues Jev) come from inventing a new task whose data must be created from scratch, as RLHF required preference data between model completions that did not exist anywhere on the internet.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Proprietary task-specific data pipelines are the moat; watch who owns novel training data for decisioning rather than who has the most GPUs.
insights.quote: before RHF existed, there was literally no human feedback data on the internet of the shape that we were looking for because we had to create it

insights.claim: Almeida argues pre-training is a bad deal unless doing something fundamentally different, because it takes exponentially more resources for debatably linear gains, and the ocean of content has already been boiled into usable models.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Bearish signal on returns to ever-larger pre-training runs; favors capital-efficient post-training players that build on open-weight models.
insights.quote: exponentially more resources for debatably linear games seems very sublinear

insights.claim: Almeida says Typesafe focuses on 10x-or-more jumps that can be made on a startup budget and believes all AI companies should be held to that bar.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Capital-efficiency thesis for AI labs; challenges the assumption that only mega-funded labs can produce frontier-relevant models.

insights.claim: Almeida claims RLVR (reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards) is by definition optimizing for benchmarks, and much of today's LLM fragility and jaggedness comes from it, with labs pouring money into in-distribution data for diminishing returns.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Suggests benchmark gains from reasoning models may overstate real-world generality; spend on RLVR data could face diminishing ROI.
insights.quote: by definition a verifiable reward is a benchmarkable

insights.claim: Almeida ranks training objectives by how easily they generalize: RLHF easiest, then RLCD, then RLVR hardest, and says RLVR models are in an extreme plateau of diminishing returns while Jev is early on its curve.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: If correct, decision-optimized models could improve faster per dollar than reasoning models for business workflows.
insights.quote: my claim is that RHFS is by far the easiest then RLCDs than RLVRs

insights.claim: Almeida guesses Claude Code's big jump around November 2025 came not from the harness itself (released months earlier and little used) but from Anthropic making a big data bet to put coding-agent behavior in the model's training distribution.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Harness/interface startups are only as good as the underlying model's in-distribution training; value accrues to whoever trains for the task, not thin wrappers.
insights.quote: My guess is this is what happened when they finally put it in distribution because you get what you optimize for

insights.claim: Almeida says OpenClaw had a powerful agent shape but suffered from unreliable intelligence, and predicts personal-assistant agents will get much better once labs put that behavior in distribution.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect a step-up in assistant-agent reliability when labs train specifically for it; a catalyst to watch for agent-product adoption.

themes.theme: Jev and RLCD: calibrated decisions as the product

insights.claim: Jev, from Typesafe, is positioned as 'machine native intelligence': a model optimized not for generating text but for reliable decisions software can act on, accessed via an API where developers supply possible decisions and inputs and receive choices with probabilities.
insights.speaker: Sam Charrington (host)
insights.so_what: A new category ('intelligence API' / decision models) that could compete with LLM APIs for high-volume backend workloads.

insights.claim: Almeida defines RLCD as the general class of algorithms that optimize specifically for calibrated decisions, contrasting it with RLHF, which he says is about pleasing humans rather than human decisions.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Calibration, not accuracy alone, is the claimed differentiator; evaluate decision-model vendors on calibration and long-tail probabilities.
insights.quote: the general class of algorithms that optimize specifically for calibrated decisions because that is what's useful for software

insights.claim: Almeida claims RLHF and RLVR immensely destroy model calibration because good string output requires extreme overconfidence via mode-dropping losses, while pre-trained base models were decently calibrated, providing seed material that RLCD bootstraps into stronger calibration.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains why chat-model probabilities are unreliable for thresholds; a technical reason specialized decision models may outperform frontier chat models on risk-sensitive automation.
insights.quote: actually RHF and RLVR destroy the calibration of the models immensely because in order to output strings well you actually need extreme overconfidence

insights.claim: Jev exposes probabilities as its knobs rather than hidden internal settings, so developers set thresholds per their own cost-benefit tradeoffs (e.g. escalation depending on customer value or current human-agent load), analogous to an LLM API returning logits for every token.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Shifts control of business policy from model vendor to developer; attractive for regulated or cost-sensitive workflows like refunds, escalation, underwriting.
insights.quote: We are basically trusting the user to make those decisions.

insights.claim: Almeida argues no function-calling API should exist without a logit bias for the function itself, and cites OpenAI's past over-refusal rollback as bad decision-making: the refuse/no-refuse decision was blended with text with no tunable threshold, so the same query could randomly refuse or not.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Points to a missing control surface in incumbent LLM APIs that a competitor or incumbent could productize.
insights.quote: no function calling API should exist without a logic bias for the function itself

insights.claim: Jev is built not by pre-training but by Frankensteining multiple open-weight models with different tradeoffs and ripping out and rejiggering fundamental pieces; Almeida says calling it post-training will likely look inaccurate in hindsight and that he specifically did not say transformers.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Typesafe depends on the open-weight ecosystem; open-weight model quality and licensing are upstream risks and enablers for this category.
insights.quote: A lot of different open source models because they all have different trade-offs to them.

insights.claim: Typesafe intentionally traded off string-generation ability, so Jev is much worse at text and its chat features are 'obviously dumb' by design.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Jev is a complement to, not replacement for, LLMs; expect hybrid stacks combining LLMs and decision models.

insights.claim: Almeida says Typesafe spent about two years in stealth, and that at the start he expected the project to take a week, given he was 'at worst tied' as the best post-trainer in the world, but discovered decision-making does not fall out of general models easily.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Suggests calibrated decisioning is technically hard, raising the barrier for quick copycats and supporting a potential moat.
insights.quote: I thought this project would take a week.

insights.claim: At OpenAI, Almeida wrote an internal document titled 'we could have had AGI last year,' arguing one year of an RLHF-scale effort could produce machine-native models; in hindsight he says RLCD was much harder than RLHF.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: The idea originated inside OpenAI; incumbents may have internal awareness and could compete directly.

insights.claim: Almeida estimates Jev today is less good at decision-making than the biggest RLVR reasoning models but much better than non-reasoning RLHF models, and expects to greatly overtake everything for business workflows as Typesafe scales up.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: A candid baseline: today Jev competes on cost/speed versus top reasoning models; the bull case requires future versions to win on quality.
insights.quote: It should be treated like an early chat GPT.

insights.claim: Almeida frames reliability gains as a lifelong journey where each added nine of reliability unlocks new categories of use cases.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Track reliability metrics, not just benchmarks, as the leading indicator of addressable automation market expansion.
insights.quote: every single nine will unlock all sorts of crazy use cases

insights.claim: Almeida says Typesafe is considering publishing its RLCD algorithms eventually, as publishing RLHF was good for the world, but not soon because the team is swamped.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: A publication would commoditize the method and accelerate competitors; watch for it as a signal of category maturation.

themes.theme: Competition, copycats and the classifier critique

insights.claim: Almeida rejects the 'it's just a classifier' critique, arguing classifiers are the shape of usefulness that powers companies like Meta and Google, and that being called a zero-shot general classifier for anything would be the greatest compliment.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Classification underpins big-tech monetization; a zero-shot general classifier could replace bespoke ML teams, a large cost line for enterprises.
insights.quote: Classifiers are an interface. Like creating classifiers is not an ML innovation.

insights.claim: Almeida pitches Jev as giving any developer the equivalent of a dozen-person 2019 ML engineering team for any task on the fly, with better quality than 2019 models.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Implies displacement of custom ML development and MLOps spend; watch for impact on traditional ML tooling vendors.

insights.claim: Within about a week of Jev's launch, half a dozen or more open-source lookalikes appeared, and OpenAI announced its own small decision models at its Dev Day.
insights.speaker: Sam Charrington (host)
insights.so_what: Rapid fast-follow from OpenAI validates the category but raises competitive risk for Typesafe; watch OpenAI decision-model adoption and pricing.

insights.claim: Almeida argues copycats, including OpenAI's decision models, focus on interface, cost and speed rather than intelligence, and that small models or embeddings plus logistic regression only deliver the intelligence of those components.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: The competitive axis Typesafe claims is calibrated intelligence; if competitors match it, Typesafe's moat narrows.
insights.quote: if you use a like a logistic regression on top of embeddings or a small model you get the intelligence of logistic regression on top of embeddings or a small model

insights.claim: Almeida calls speed and cost 'bad things' to be minimized, and says reliability is what customers actually pay for; he worries poor copycat models could burn developers on the whole subgenre.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Category reputation risk: low-quality entrants could slow adoption of decision models broadly.
insights.quote: reliability is what people are paying for

insights.claim: Almeida says investors who recently called his pitch the greatest they had heard rejected the identical pitch a year earlier, arguing they are reacting to product-market fit rather than the idea.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Typesafe is actively fundraising after launch traction; signals hot investor demand for the decision-model category.
insights.quote: What you guys are reacting to is the product market fit.

insights.claim: Almeida says the first wave of Jev enthusiasts were structured-output practitioners such as the DSPy community, who were intellectually right but hobbled by string-optimized models; cost-savings seekers were the second wave.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Early adopters are programmatic-AI developers; developer-community traction is the leading indicator to monitor.
insights.quote: like a phantom lib was returned

insights.claim: Almeida says Typesafe chose not to name the category 'decision models' because the model class covers more than decisions, hinting at undisclosed roadmap capabilities and upcoming 'system one models' and multiple models.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Roadmap expansion beyond classification could widen TAM; watch for early-access program and multi-model launches.
insights.quote: there's a lot more that fits this class of models beyond decisions

themes.theme: Software architecture: models as nodes, not harnesses

insights.claim: Almeida rejects the agent-harness concept as a 'horseless carriage' attempt to make intelligence look human, arguing instead that Jev is a low-level component embedded in user code, like a node in an n8n-style workflow, with users owning logic and data.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Benefits workflow/orchestration platforms and developer-tool ecosystems; challenges the 'agent does everything' thesis behind many valuations.
insights.quote: I just reject the notion of harness entirely.

insights.claim: Almeida notes it is unusual for an API to require customers to send their whole business algorithm in a system prompt to someone else's server, and envisions intelligence becoming like databases, called from code when needed.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Data-privacy and IP concerns favor narrow intelligence APIs over prompt-heavy LLM agents for enterprise adoption.
insights.quote: one day intelligence will be like databases where you just call it when you need it

insights.claim: Almeida argues Waymo is the gold standard for self-driving and safer than Tesla because it decomposes systems into engineered, understood components, framing it as an engineering win rather than an AI win and a model for reliable AI systems.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports modular, engineered AI over end-to-end approaches for safety-critical deployments; relevant to the Waymo vs Tesla autonomy debate.
insights.quote: I see self-driving as a ginormous engineering win, not necessarily an AI win.

insights.claim: Almeida argues reliable automation for high-value, background, or high-volume workflows should be engineered up front and maintained, while one-off just-in-time tasks are fine for unreliable LLMs; hybrids like LLM-written workflows that call Jev across many documents are a middle ground.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Market segmentation: agentic LLMs for ad hoc work, decision models for scaled background automation; both can coexist.
insights.quote: it's a feature for automation. It is not a feature for just in time stuff.

insights.claim: Almeida argues agent design is heavily constrained by expensive, append-only KV caches, which prevent patterns like fan-out, filtering, reordering and hierarchical lookups within context; cheap reliable intelligence could enable very different agent architectures.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Inference-cost structure shapes agent product design; cheaper per-decision intelligence could unlock new agent architectures and change inference demand patterns.
insights.quote: How would you design a coding agent if KV caching didn't exist?

insights.claim: Almeida says tool calls cause context rot, and models overfit to native harnesses tend to call native tools far more than plugged-in ones; logit biases on tool calls could give fine-grained control without poisoning context.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Third-party tool vendors integrated into frontier-lab agents may see lower invocation than expected; a structural disadvantage versus native tools.
insights.quote: because the models have been overfit to their native harnesses, they tend to call the native tools a lot more than the ones you plug in

insights.claim: Almeida predicts the future will be hybrids where software progressively latches onto agent harnesses like Claude Code and Codex until systems become much more software and much less magic loop.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect gradual migration of agent logic into deterministic code; benefits tooling that bridges agents and conventional software.

insights.claim: Almeida says Typesafe considered building its own products, including a design for using Jev in coding agents, but decided not to and instead focus on being a developer platform.
insights.speaker: Diego Almeida (Typesafe CEO)
insights.so_what: Typesafe is positioned as infrastructure rather than an application competitor, making it a potential partner to agent companies.
